query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A low‐level tungsten microalloying (≈0.5 at.%) in the CoCrFeNi alloy will enable the formation of finely dispersed W‐rich intermetallics that boost room‐temperature hardness and, crucially, enhance tribo-oxidation at elevated temperatures (up to 800 °C) to form a continuous, protective oxide (glaze) layer. This in situ–formed lubricious layer is expected to stabilize the friction coefficient and lower the wear rate throughout the full sliding temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy in its cast or sintered state, exhibiting its characteristic phase structure and moderate wear performance across the temperature range.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 0.5 at.% tungsten into the CoCrFeNi matrix via alloying (e.g., by powder metallurgy, laser cladding, or other processing routes).
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests conducted from room temperature (≈25 °C) to 800 °C under atmospherical conditions, with contact pressures typical for ball-on-disk tribometers (e.g., around 0.9–1.0 GPa) and loads representative of engineering applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The tungsten addition is expected to promote fine W-rich intermetallic precipitates and increase lattice distortion, which serve as nucleation sites for a stable, high-temperature oxide glaze layer comprising, for example, tungsten oxide species blended with existing oxides from the base alloy.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the microalloying with W increases hardness and refines the microstructure, reducing adhesive and abrasive wear. At elevated temperatures, the W-rich phases facilitate tribo-oxidation by providing continuous nucleation sites for a lubricious oxide layer. This glaze layer minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby lowering friction and mitigating severe wear even as the substrate softens.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi, the tungsten-alloyed variant will show a lower and more stable coefficient of friction and significantly reduced wear rates (potentially by up to an order of magnitude at 800 °C), with improved performance consistency across the entire temperature span.
generation.baseline: The baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, without tungsten, tends to exhibit higher friction variability and increased wear—especially at elevated temperatures—due to less robust oxide formation and lower hardness.
generation.boundary: This strategy is expected to be effective under dry, ambient (oxidizing) conditions in the specified temperature range. Excess tungsten or processing routes that do not yield a uniform microstructure might disrupt the beneficial phase formation. In highly reducing environments or under conditions of extreme thermal shock, the protective oxide layer may not form as predicted.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis extrapolates from evidence in tungsten-alloyed AlCoCrFeNiWx coatings (see PMC8470387) and assumes similar benefits in a simpler CoCrFeNi system. It is uncertain how the oxide‐forming kinetics and intermetallic stability in CoCrFeNi will compare and whether the protective glaze layer will be as continuous. Further microstructural and tribological analysis across the full temperature range is required to validate the proposed benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of pure CoCrFeNi and another set microalloyed with ~0.5 at.% tungsten using an identical processing route. Conduct systematic ball-on-disk sliding wear tests at incremental temperatures (e.g., RT, 150 °C, 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C) under identical dry, ambient conditions. Characterize the microstructure before and after testing using SEM, TEM, and XRD, and quantify the oxide layer formation via EDS mapping.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) curves at each test temperature
Microstructural analysis of worn surfaces (characterizing oxide/glaze layer continuity and intermetallic phase dispersion)
Hardness testing at room temperature and after high-temperature exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-alloyed CoCrFeNi shows no statistically significant reduction in COF and wear rate across the temperature range compared to the baseline, or if the protective oxide layer is discontinuous or absent (as determined by post-test microstructural analyses), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractFriction and wear properties of hot working die steel at above 800 °C are of particular interest for high temperature applications. Here, novel AlCoCrFeNiWx high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings have been fabricated on the surface of hot working die steel by laser cladding. The effects of the as-prepared AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings on the microstructure and high temperature friction and wear behavior of hot working die steel are investigated through scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS). Having benefited from the formation of W-rich intermetallic compounds after the addition of W elements, the high temperature wear resistance of the coatings is obviously improved, and friction coefficient shows a large fluctuation. The microstructural characteristics of the AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings after the high temperature wear resistance test shows a highly favorable impact on microstructure stability and wear resistance, due to its the strong lattice distortion effect of W element on BCC solid solutions and the second phase strengthening of the W-rich intermetallic compounds. cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 shows the influence of the W powder addition on the high temperature friction and wear properties of the AlCoCrFeNiWx coatings on H13 steel. The H13 steel exhibits a maximum friction coefficient and wear loss after 800 °C/60 min high temperature friction and wear treatment. Compared to the H13 steel, all HEA coatings exhibit smaller friction coefficient and wear loss. A minimum friction coefficient and wear loss (only 12% of H13 steel wear loss) occurs in the AlCoCrFeNiWx with the addition of 0.5 at.% W. Consequently, a great improvement in the high temperature friction and wear resistance is achieved by the addition of the W powder and is likely due to the lattice distortion becoming more remarkable; the unmelted W-rich particles also improve the wear resistance as the hard phase. The addition of 0.5 at.% W powder in AlCoCrFeNi HEA system can improve its high temperature friction and wear resistance. These results are also supported by wear scars height and width of samples. The distinct differences are observed with regard to three-dimensional morphologies, as shown in Figure 7.
